utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness will be giving evidence for the events that occurred in Urosevac municipality again, so the Kosovo atlas map is on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name to the Court, sir.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: My name is Avni Nebihu, Ferizaj municipality, Sojevo village. I was born on 12 April, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you an Albanian and a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes. I am Albanian from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I work in the transportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Nebihu, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on May the 2nd, 1999, and again on 20 November, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, you provided them with two statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And on the 5th of February this year, 2002, you attended a meeting and you appeared before a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal, and you were provided with an Albanian copy, a copy in the Albanian language of your statement. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you reviewed the statements at that time?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution submits the two statements under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 139.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The summary of the witness's testimony is the following: The witness comes from the village of Sojevo in the municipality of Urosevac. He testifies that starting with the NATO airstrikes on 24 March 1999, Serb forces were moving along the main road and firing in the direction of the houses in his village. Four to five days later, the Serb army arrived at the witness's village and took up positions around the school and at the mosque. The witness saw four large tanks and at least three APCs, a large number of soldiers wearing olive-green colour uniforms. Within 30 minutes of their arrival, the soldiers started shooting in the air. They were later joined by paramilitaries, and the witness believes the army and the paramilitaries were working in concert. Two days after they entered the village, the soldiers started forcibly removing people from their homes. Three APCs and soldiers on foot arrived at the witness's house. The witness started to move his family towards the woods and was followed by an APC which constantly shot into the air. Approximately 400 villagers gathered in the woods. The soldiers set fire to all the houses, and the villagers in the woods were soon surrounded by paramilitaries who robbed them and left. Most of the villagers headed for Urosevac using the back roads. The witness and his family stayed in Urosevac for about a week, during which the army kept a very tight control of the city. The witness's brother came to the house where the witness was staying because soldiers had entered the house where he was staying, beat everybody up, lined them up for execution, and forced them to leave the house. The witness attempted to return to his village, but he was told that his uncle and his uncle's wife had been killed and so decided to return to Urosevac. On April 12, the witness and his family went to the train station and were taken to Djeneral Jankovic. When the witness and others disembarked from the train, Serb army and police were present. They directed them to walk down the railway tracks into Macedonia. That's all, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your first statement, you claim that in your village there were about 200 houses, and in every one of these houses there were nine or ten people, as you had put it. Is that to say that the population of your village was between 1.800 and 2.000? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me the exact date when you left your village together with the other villagers.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We left the village on 6th of March. I'm sorry, on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, you claim that the village of Sojevo, on that day when you left the village, that actually about 500 villagers left together with you. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I can't hear well. I can't hear interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we just check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you hear the last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was that, in your statement, you referred to leaving the village with about 500 other villagers, and you were asked, "Is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, you said that you know that only 11 villagers stayed back in the village when you left. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I said that 11 inhabitants were killed. I didn't say 11 stayed behind. There were more left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Some didn't manage to flee, some stayed, and 11 were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: No one remained behind in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No one stayed behind in the village? Five hundred people left together with you. Awhile ago, we said that the population was about 2.000. And what happened with the remaining 1.500 villagers?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I didn't say 1.000 or 2.000, but I said we were a group who left the neighbours'. Together with the guests we had, we were about 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But at the outset, we stated that in the village there were about 1.800 -- between 1.800 and 2.000 people. If 500 left in your group, what -- and nobody stayed behind in the village, what happened to the remaining 1.300 or 1.500 who are missing?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, we were about 500 people, and the regular army drove us out of our homes, and we had to leave. And they started to set fire on the houses. We were about 500 metres away. We stopped a little while further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you and see that there is no confusion here. The point which is being made is that you left the village with 500 or so. Can you tell us what happened to the others from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village is spread out. It has several neighbourhoods. I am testifying about what happened in my neighbourhood. I have no information about other neighbourhoods, but I can tell you about what happened in my own neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did anybody stay behind from your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two people remained behind. In another neighbourhood close by, there were two other people who were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we now establish what happened with the remaining 1.500 villagers? You're talking about 11, you're talking about five, you're talking about 500. What happened with the remaining 1.500? The population of the village was between 1.800 and 2.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already explained that in fact he's dealing with his neighbourhood alone. That's what he can give evidence about. He says he can't give evidence about the rest of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me clarify this matter. Mr. Nebihu, you wrote in your statement that Sojevo is a village with about 200 houses. How many houses were there in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 30, 31, 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again our figures do not match, because if it's 30 houses, then about 300 people could have left with him according to the data the witness has provided. Now we've started dividing villages in terms of neighbourhoods, closer and further neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We did not divide the villages, but they are, the village is like that; it is separated in different neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that when you gave your first statement you confirmed that you would testify only about what happened to you or about events that you witnessed yourself? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I will testify only to what I went through and to what I saw with my own eyes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Why are you then testifying about Ekrem Etemi and Naser Etemi and their alleged wounding when you never saw their wounding and you never saw who wounded them and you never saw where they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We were in the village. They were killed on the main road, Gjilan-Ferizaj. A military car of yours stopped them. It was a white car. The people were dressed in military uniforms, and they asked them about the names, and -- and then they shot them with a pistol. The villagers who were there with them, nearby, took them, that is, their buddies. They wanted to take them to Macedonia. Naser managed to be taken to Macedonia. The other one was returned -- was taken to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, awhile ago you said they were killed. In your statement, you said that they were wounded. Now, again, you're saying that they were wounded.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I said they were shot but not shot dead. I met Naser in Stankovac after he was recovered from the wounds, and I saw with my own eyes the bullet that they had taken out of his bullet [as interpreted]. But with Ekrem, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know where he left; right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They left on that day. Ekrem was taken to Pristina hospital; the other one to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, you claim that you were standing in front of your house when the soldiers entered your brother's house. In your second statement, you claim that you were standing in the yard and that you were actually watching what was going on. Where were you actually standing?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We were in the yard when they entered the house. And two officers they were. They said to him, "Hold up your hands." We were there, watching what was going on. Then they drove out of his house my brother and all of us, and we left all together. We gathered about 500 away from that place [as interpreted]. Then we saw our houses set on fire immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to that later. Where were you standing then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he was in the yard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, on page 3, paragraph 5, you still claim that when you saw what was going on in the neighbouring houses, you entered your own house, and you said to your family that you had to go. Is it correct that that is what you stated, that that's the way things happened?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes. This is what happened. The soldiers entered the yard and told us, "What are you waiting for? Why don't you leave?" And we asked them, "Where are we going?" They said, "Do you expect us to tell you where you should go?" That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify precisely what you've said just now. Awhile ago, I put a question to you. I said in your statement you claimed that when you saw what was going on in the neighbouring houses, you entered your own house and you said to your family that you had to go. Is that the way it was? That is to say, when you saw this -- this is your claim: When you saw what was going on in the neighbouring houses, you entered your house and you said to your family that you had to go. Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: No. That is not true. No. No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Take a look at this paragraph here, in the middle of the penultimate paragraph. Before that, you actually describe what was going on and what your brother said to you, that they had searched him, et cetera. "In the immediate neighbourhood of my house, there were six other houses, and they went to another house. The soldiers were throwing families out of their houses." And now I'm telling you what you claim you did not say. "When I saw what was going on, I decided not to wait. I went in and told my family that we had to leave. I started to move my family out of the house, and we headed towards the woods." So you say here that when you saw what was going on, you went into the house and said to your family that you had to leave. That is what you claim now that you had not said. In the other statement, you say that the soldiers came and said to you, "What are you waiting for? Why don't you leave your house?" Now, what is correct out of all of this? Did you see what was happening and did you enter the house and tell your family you had to leave or was it the soldiers who came to you and said, "What are you waiting for? Go." These are two completely different things that you've been saying in these two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I saw my brother taken out of his house, I saw two armoured cars stopped in front of the yard. Then the brother came to my home, accompanied by the soldiers, and an officer told me, "Why have you shut the door?" I didn't say a word. And he said, "Go away. Why are you waiting any more?" That was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference between these two statements of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his explanation. If you want to make a comment, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, you say that you left the house with your family and went -- and took to the woods, headed towards the woods; and in your second statement, you say that you were escorted by the soldiers who had ordered you to leave and that they in fact took you to Poljane where there was a group of paramilitaries. Which of the two is correct; what you said in your first statement or what you said in your second?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: It was the regular army that drove us out of our homes. Then they escorted us as the villagers who were getting together, with the armoured cars, about 500 metres away, and then they set fire to our houses. After an hour, the paramilitaries came, and we took a position further, and from there, we watched our houses burning. Then after that, they divided us in two groups; the women and children in one group, the males in another group. They took away the valuables, jewellery, necklaces, whatever the women had. You know yourself. And we happened to know some one of them, and I addressed him. He told us, "Don't talk to me in Albanian. Talk to me in Serbian, because they may understand what you are saying." [As interpreted]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you a few direct questions now because I don't feel that we're understanding each other with respect to the differences in your statement. So I'm going to read out the passage that relates to the same event in your first and second statement, and perhaps that will be easier for you. You'll be able to answer my questions more easily. For example, in the first statement, you say the following: "In the night when NATO first started its bombing, I went outside together with other members of my family to watch it. I had quite a number of guests staying in my house at the time." I have been asked to read more slowly. "That was on the 24th of March. It was around midnight, and we were in the yard. I heard shots coming from the direction of the main road running to Urosevac. I saw some inflammatory bullets coming from that direction, and it appeared as if they were shooting in the direction of the houses on both sides and also up in the air. I wasn't able to see who was doing the shooting." In your second statement, you say the following: "When the NATO bombing started, the Serb forces were moving along the main road and were shooting in the direction of the houses in my village. Some of the bullets hit the houses belonging to my cousins, but there were no casualties." So in your first statement, you describe NATO bombing, and you saw these illuminating bullets and the anti-aircraft artillery, although you also say that you thought they were shooting in the direction of the houses. In your second statement, you say that the forces were moving along the main road and that they were shooting at the houses and that, "a certain number of bullets hit the houses belonging to my cousins although there were no casualties." Now, which of those two statements is correct; what you said in the first or what you said in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I contend that both statements are the same. After the NATO bombing started, they shelled the village all the night. And that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose the question can be put in this way: In your first statement, you did not mention the bullets hitting your cousin's house. Was there any reason for that, as to why you didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I -- I believe that in the first statement they were only asking me about that day on which we left, after the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you about the second difference that I think is far more essential. In your first statement, you talk about one of the soldiers, whom you identify as being Novica Mijovic and who helped you there. But that's not the point, nor is the point that you make no mention of him in the second statement. I'm going to read a portion of your first statement, on page 4, where you say the following: "Thanks to Novica, we are still alive. There were about 400 of us villagers at this point. One of the soldiers told us that we had to separate the men from the women. It was then that Novica told us in Albanian not to talk to him in Serbian because they would understand what we were talking about. He told us to speak to him only in Albanian. They told us to sit on the ground in a very tight group. There were in total about 30 to 40 of these soldiers." And then we come to my question. I have read the whole paragraph so that you can get the context. Then you say: "Novica spoke to one of the other soldiers and had them change their minds about separating the men and the women." Full stop. "We were allowed to stay together." You say that in your first statement. So in your first statement, you say this, explaining who helped you, and you go on to explain that they did not separate you, and you clearly state that you were allowed to stay together. In your second statement, the last paragraph on page 1, you say the following: "When the paramilitaries surrounded us and stopped us, we were close to the village of Grlica in the woods. Their first words were women and children to separate from men." Then you go on to state the following: "When they separated us--" that is to say you claim that they did in fact separate you -- "the women were robbed of their money and jewellery and they even took a ring from my brother. The soldiers kept us there for 15 to 20 minutes before they all left," and so on. "We did not know where to go. We had heard..." Et cetera. So in your first statement, you claim that they did not separate you and that thanks to this man whom you mention, a Serb by the name of Novica Mijovic, they let you stay together. They didn't separate you, you were allowed to stay together. However, in your second statement, you say that they did separate you and that then they proceeded to take your money and jewellery. So the point that has to be clarified is: Did they separate you or did they not separate you? Are you clear on the fact that in your first statement you state that they did not separate you and in your second you state that they did separate you? Now, can there be any misunderstanding there about giving two quite different statements? Are you clear on the fact that you in fact gave two quite different statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should be given copies of these statements so that he can see -- so that he can see. You're putting that they're different. He should have copies so that he can tell what's in them. Has he got copies? Very well. I wonder if the usher would help him to find his way round. The first -- the first statement, it's on page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence of that second paragraph states: "We were allowed to stay together. They changed their minds about separating the men and the women, and we were allowed to stay together." That's what it says. And also, in the last paragraph on page 1 of the second statement, it says: "When they separated us --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's start with the first statement. Mr. Nebihu, can you find the passage which begins, "Thanks to Novica, we are still alive"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That seems to me page 5, second paragraph in the Albanian statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what idea he had, but he helped us as far as he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And everything -- and everything that I said, that he was intending to help us, and that he did his best to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read that paragraph and the next one which begins, "Three or four of these soldiers went to every person in the group and demanded our money. They also took the jewellery from the women." Can you find those two paragraphs? Just read them for the moment. Just read the two over to yourself and then you'll be asked some questions about another statement. Have you read those two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now you're going to be shown your second statement. Have you got the second statement there? The first page of the full statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It's page 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 3 of the Albanian. Would you find the paragraph which begins, "When the paramilitaries surrounded us and stopped us, we were close to the village of Grlica, in the woods." If you'd read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph of page 3 in the Albanian statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe if you give the statement -- if the usher gives the statement to the Prosecution, they can find it, or perhaps the Registrar can help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just read that paragraph. Now, the point which is being made is that in the first statement, you say that Novica spoke to one of the other soldiers and had them change their minds about separating the men and the women. You were allowed to stay together. And then you go on to say that, after that, you were robbed, you and the women. In the second statement, it says that, "Their first words were, women and children to separate from men. When they separated us, the women were robbed of their money." And the point which is being made is that in the first statement it appears that you are saying you were all allowed to stay together. In the second, it said -- it appears to say that you were separated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said they separated us, that is, men from women, that they looted the women, that they robbed them of their jewellery. Then they took away my brother's ring. Someone said, "Give it away, because they might be problems from us." And then we asked, "Where are we going now? Where should we go now?" And he said to us, "You should go in the direction of Ferizaj." We couldn't go to Skopje because we were on foot. That's why we went to Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Concentrate on the separation. Did you remain separated, the men from the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, we were separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you were together again or not, or did you remain separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment came when we got together again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. The usher can return. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Have we cleared this up then? Did they separate you or not?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: They separated us. I think I've said it three times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why then in your first statement did you say that they did not separate you?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I didn't say that they didn't separate us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, "We were allowed to stay together."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's fair to the witness, in light of the answer that he gave the Presiding Judge. It's a question of sequence. What he said is that they were separated first and they came together at some time after that. I think essentially in these matters of discrepancies, once the explanation is given, the matter should end. It is for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight we will attach to the witness's evidence in the light of the discrepancy and the explanation given. Once the explanation has been given, I think you should move on and leave the rest to us to determine the weight to attach to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. If that is your job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the first statement, you say on that same page but one paragraph further on, that: "The soldiers then left us. Novica allowed us to go to our vehicles and tractors. We then immediately left, and together we headed towards Urosevac using the backroads." In your second statement, at the end of that same paragraph where you had been talking about how you were separated and looted, robbed, at the end of that paragraph, you said that you went on foot and that a group had a vehicle but that you yourself went on foot. You said, "I was on foot." Now, did you go to your vehicles and tractors? Because you say you went up to your vehicles and tractors and then took the backroads to Urosevac, whereas in your second statement you say you went on foot. So which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: The truth is that personally, I didn't have a vehicle, but some of the villagers had their carts and tractors, and they went and took them, and some of us were on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At the end of your first statement -- or, rather, let me start with your second statement. You say on that morning -- this is towards the end of your second statement. It's a short paragraph, and you say: "That morning, at the station, there were no uniformed policemen unless they were in civilian clothes, but there was movement of military and police on the road close to the station. Inside the station, nobody was telling us what to do." That is that whole paragraph. Now, in the last paragraph of your first statement, this is what you say: "We all went to the train station early in the morning. There were a lot of people at the station. There were four rail cars. No one asked for documentation or tickets. There were a lot of policemen in their regular police uniforms. They didn't do anything to the people going to the train station. We got onto the train which took us to Djeneral Jankovic. Once there, we got off the train. The police there directed us to walk down the railway tracks into Macedonia. We were never asked for documentation. We still have our documents." So that is that particular paragraph. Now, my question for you is the following: In the second statement, you say quite resolutely that there were no uniformed policemen. In your first statement, you state there were a lot of policemen in their regular police uniforms. Can you explain that, too, that difference?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: The truth is that there were policemen. I mean when we got onto the train. But then they were on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your explanation about the differences in the two statements, that there were no policemen and that there were a lot of policemen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given the explanation that there were policemen on the train.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not what it says in the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but that's his explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the first statement, you say that when you were moving into the woods with your family, you were followed by an APC from which -- which shot into the air above your heads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: That happened when we left our houses. We had armoured vehicles behind us. So please don't mix up the village with the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not mixing it up. I'm just asking you different questions. Now, this question was that you say that when you were moving towards the woods with your family, that that's when this took place.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: When we left our houses, we were followed by auto vehicles until the point when we were outside the village and then we stood positioned, ready to return. And then the paramilitaries followed us and then we were helped by Novica and that is the point where --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I've moved on to some other questions now linked to the APC, the armoured personnel carrier that followed you. In your second statement, you make no mention of the APC. In your second statement, you say that when they threw you out of your houses, that a group of paramilitary forces arrived in the village in three buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealing with a different point there. He's given his account and this is a second statement. Now, unless there's a discrepancy, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that, from the woods, you saw the soldiers set fire to your houses. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We were not present actually at the place when they set fire, but we saw it from afar when we were gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that you saw the houses being set fire to with some device that lets out fire. Now, I'm asking you about this. You say you saw this from the woods and now you say that you couldn't see this directly. How then can you say that you saw what they were using to set your houses alight when you couldn't even see the houses properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't say he couldn't see the houses properly. What he said is, "We weren't present actually at the place when they set it on fire but we saw it from afar." Now could you see how they were setting the houses on fire, Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Nebihu, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After they drove us away from our houses, we were about only 500 metres away. If we were at home, they would have burned us alive too, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just -- just listen to the question, please. Were you able to see how the Serb forces were setting fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't see that because we were not in the place. We only saw the smoke and the flames coming out of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you to go to Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Novica told us, "I think it's best. It's best for you to go to Ferizaj and not stay there as a group. I mean walk as a group. Do not separate, because you'll be safer in this way."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The part of Urosevac where you were staying was quiet, wasn't it? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It was calm. In one place where we were staying, we stayed there for a week. Women went out to fetch food and stuffs because we men were afraid. Then after six days, we left early in the morning by train and went to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is this quiet area from the centre of town, this quiet area that you were staying at?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: About one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About a kilometre? You claim that during those days, NATO had bombed. Could you hear NATO bombings from town?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was NATO bombing in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I don't know what it bombed in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many people were killed by the NATO bombings during those days in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I don't think there was anyone killed by NATO bombing. At least, I don't know and I don't think it's true that anyone was killed as a result of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. When did you leave Urosevac? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: On 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: March?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's some kind of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 12th of April. And you say that you left your village on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We left the village on the 6th of April. For six days, we stayed in Ferizaj, and then on the 12th, being unable to stay there any longer, we had to leave Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 6th of April, as far as I could understand, you left the village because our forces expelled you and torched your houses. Is that right? That is briefly what you had claimed.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I said on the 6th of April we left the village and on the 12th of April, we entered Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know of the village of Mirosavlje?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I know that some houses were burned there, but I can't give any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is Mirosavlje from Sojevo?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We are neighbours because our village is rather spread out, as I said earlier. Not very far -- not very close, I would say. It's a bit farther.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because yesterday -- I'm asking you this because yesterday, a witness from Mirosavlje claimed that he first saw fires from your village on the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot comment on what some other witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking him to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is do you know exactly when this happened, this that you have been asserting?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: The truth is that on the 6th, the houses were set on fire, but the fact is also that the fire went on for one or two days. So it's not that they were set on fire for one hour or two hours, you know. They continued to issue smoke and flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. In your first statement, you claim that without any problems whatsoever, you left by train to Djeneral Jankovic, but in the second statement, you claim that you had to pay ten Deutschmarks per person. So which one of the two is correct? Did you have to pay or did you not have to pay?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I didn't mention this in the first statement because they didn't ask me. But in the second, I said that some people had to pay, let's say up to 10 marks, Deutschmarks, and some didn't have to pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did they pay this money to? Did they have tickets issued to them by a conductor? Who did they give this money to?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: There were many people. I can't say who got tickets or whether they got tickets. As far as I am concerned, I didn't receive any tickets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you pay?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you give these ten Deutschmarks to?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I paid that money at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To whom? You said that you paid, but you did not get a ticket. Who did you give the money to?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I paid the money at the station. The ticket --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Who was it that you gave the money to when you paid at the station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who sells tickets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now over, unless there's one more question you want to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have only a few questions left, so I think I can finish, because I have not overstepped the time. I have a minute or two left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have a minute or two and no more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do have an objection as well, so I do hope that there will not be included in this time. So I'll start with the objection. When this witness was introduced, the explanation was given that he gave two statements, one on the 2nd of May, 1999 and one in November, 2001. And this statement -- the second statement of the 20th of November, 2001, on the first page one can see that there was yet another statement that was given on the 28th of August, 2001, that is to say, three months before that. How is it possible that this side across the well can put different statements together into one statement and without cautioning, while introducing the witness, that there were three statements altogether, and who combined these statements that are given here? So gentlemen - Mr. May, Mr. Robinson, and Mr. Kwon - please look at this first page. It says: Date of interviews: The 29th of August, 2001 and the 20th of November, 2001. Two statements within three months' time put together in one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: If I can clarify. The second statement is the product of the interviews which took place on the 29th of August and again on the 20th of November. There is no third statement whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Now, you have two minutes more to ask questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give your statement in the following way: Did you yourself talk about what had happened to you or did you answer questions?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I said only what happened and then I made the necessary corrections. They asked me whether that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say that they did not put any questions to you except for asking whether that was true.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: They asked me questions and then they said to me, "You have to say the same thing in all the statements," and this is how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the investigator ask you why you had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: We left Kosova on your orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether the investigator asked you why you had left Kosovo. The man who talked to you, the man you gave your statement to, did he ask you why you had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did he ask you -- did he ask you whether you were pleased by the fact that NATO had bombed? Did he put that question to you?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: In fact, we welcomed NATO bombing because there was no other way we could have stayed in our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether this man who talked to you asked you whether you were pleased by the fact that NATO had bombed.

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: He asked me, and I said yes, I was happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me a minute. Mr. Nebihu, I'm a little bit confused about the date. What was the date when you left Urosevac or Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it seems to me that in both of your statements it was 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a mistake. I told them 12th of April. When they read the statement to me, I said, "You have to correct this mistake, because it was the 12th of April." But probably they have not corrected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Nebihu, I would like to clarify the fact -- the event that happened when your -- when you were in your house and when the soldiers approached your brother's gate of your house, and that was the events that took place at that moment were the events that lead you to leave your house. And I think that when Mr. Milosevic asked you some questions, there were -- there were -- there was a little bit of confusion why did you leave your house. Can you please go back to this fact and explain to the Court again how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: This happened when they entered the yard of my brother's house. I was outside, and I saw everything. They drove out the family of my brother. They were unable to take anything with them, any clothes or anything. And then together with my brother, we left because they told us, "Why aren't you leaving? What are you waiting for?"

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And when you say "they," you are referring to whom?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I'm talking about my brother, my brother's family, my own family, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because we live in the same compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Nebihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just have one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When you were in the woods, Mr. Nebihu, and you saw from that place, you saw -- you saw the soldiers setting fire to the houses, and when asked if you could see how they did that, you said you were not able to see. In your first statement, you said that you saw some kind of weapon that the soldiers were carrying and that was throwing fire. Was that a mistake or did you see that weapon?

utterances.speaker: AVNI NEBIHU
utterances.text: I saw the weapons when they captured us, but I didn't see the weapon they used to set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nebihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nebihu, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have private session for a short period to return to the topic that we covered yesterday morning first thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An expert, Dr. Baccard, is due to give evidence on the 21st. His statement has been served under the appropriate provisions. We can't expect any formalities from the accused. We can't speak to the accused directly, and so far those lawyers who are assisting him haven't taken the opportunity to get in touch with me. Therefore, we should know and invite the Chamber to assist us in learning whether the accused wishes him to attend for cross-examination or not. If he is to attend for cross-examination on good grounds, then the logistics for bringing him here and allowing him to review the material in advance of giving his evidence will have to be made, all of which is going to be quite labour and time-consuming. If not, then his report can be simply read or taken as read on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is an expert on exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's been suggested --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The evidence of Dr. Baccard, who is an expert on exhumations, is before the Court in the form of a report. Do you want to cross-examine that witness or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for that question to be posed with respect to any of the witnesses because I am here -- I said here in public on many occasions that witnesses who I'm not able to cross-examination, secret witnesses and so on and so forth, cannot be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What is the position? He's an expert. If there is -- if there is a call for cross-examination, then I think the Court's powers are limited, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's Rule 94, I think. Within 14 days of the filing of the statement of the expert witness - well, that time's long expired, I'm afraid - the opposing party shall file a notice indicating whether it accepts the expert's statement or wishes to cross-examine. If the party accepts the statement, the statement may be admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber without calling the witness to testify. That's the Rule as earlier drafted, and I -- those parts of it haven't been amended in the latest amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you will have his report put before the Court, presumably, and he must be here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is extremely unfortunate that the accused is not prepared, himself or by his lawyers, to consider witnesses on a case-by-case basis and that he should seek simply to exert by blanket bar or blanket approach to the witnesses to exert this effect on the timetable of this trial, but the answer is we'll have him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I still repeat that it would be helpful if those lawyers who are assisting him can get in touch. They have duties to the Court to which they have signed. The second point, I understand that the Court and its officers have been inconvenienced, perhaps substantially, by the changes in witness orders that have been happening recently, and I'm very sorry if that's been the case. Of course, it's largely if not wholly circumstances outside our control with the particular timetable, to which we're responding, that lead to these changes but it's vital we do everything we can to keep you and your staff alert. I'm instituting a new procedure where I will have before you, if not today, tomorrow, a list right to the end of trial of a witness order, and whenever there's a change, even on a daily basis, we will resubmit the document with, I don't know, italicised or bolded or underlined, the changes; and we hope that this will reduce or avoid altogether the inconvenience to which your staff has previously been subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow, K4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Romano reminds me that he is included in the list of witnesses for whom the 92 bis provisions generally have been sought, and I think he may now prove to be the first one of that batch to whom our application relates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter, while it's in mind, is this, and that is the formalities of Rule 92 bis should not be overlooked in these submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I think I explained when I first raised it as a possibility that of course there would be necessary abbreviation of time, but I don't know if those are the formalities that you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course it's because of those provisions and the need to abbreviate the time that we drew to your attention, to the attention of the accused, that he will have been provided in advance with statements, a long time in advance, to read so there can be no prejudice, and we, of course, reminded you in the application that the procedure has, I think, been adopted in one other Trial Chamber in any event. It's a method of saving time. We commend it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there's a matter I wanted to ask you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about. In relation to the testimony of the vast majority of the witnesses, we have two statements. There's a first statement and then there's a second statement coming much later after the first, usually much closer to the trial. The accused has quite rightly been cross-examining on discrepancies that arise between the two statements. I wanted to find out from you what was the strategy, what was being aimed at by the investigators or by the OTP in general in getting these second statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a matter better dealt with by one of the investigators or the lead investigator when he comes, because it's not something which I necessarily deal with in detail. But I think the answer will be along these lines: That the earlier statements may have been taken as part of a general inquiry, and when the decision is made that the particular witness is to be listed for a particular case, he's seen again. And all too often, not only are the matters that need to be clarified in relation to the original statement, but the witness himself will recall and bring up other matters that need to be covered. So I suspect it's a two-part process. And indeed it's in the nature of events, as we discovered from the 92 bis witnesses, that witnesses, at the time they're first seen, rarely remember or are reminded of all matters that are material, and they frequently come to court, even when 92 bis'd, with further photographs and further details that they've forgotten to tell us about. And with the best of all conceivable investigation techniques, it seems that this is going to carry on happening. So I suspect that the second statements are usually a combination of us seeking details and them remembering further material. Ms. Romano might be going to give me a further reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I am reminded, helpfully, that, of course, the first statements were very often taken in camps of one kind or another in circumstances where it is very difficult, if not possible, to expect the best out of witnesses whose minds are probably concentrated on things other, frankly, than trying to go about perfect recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps just one other matter. I'm sorry, Mr. Kay, but while it's in the mind. Next week we should -- we have your latest document on proposals for the rest of this part of the trial - numbers of witnesses and the like - and we are considering it, and we ought to have a session on it sometime next week when we can find a convenient time to discuss it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think next week we're not sitting on the Friday. We're sitting on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, I think. We have -- I'm going to be here, I think, all next week. We have witnesses on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, who are substantial in time probably, and content, it might be prudent not to interrupt those witnesses, not to interrupt in the middle of the course of either of them. There's Mr. Drewienkiewicz, who comes back just for a couple of hours, and there's a witness who will probably take some time, starting after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will not interrupt the witnesses, and if it's not possible next week, we will do it the week after, but we ought to have the matter in mind. Mr. Kay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's more of a point of observation. It concerns the statement of Dr. Eric Baccard, served as an expert witness. My records show that was served the 16th of April, and we're now the 8th of May. So the 30-day period for the accused has not expired in relation to that matter, which I thought the Trial Chamber ought to know since there's been some criticism of him in relation to how he deals with advance notice of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. A moment ago you noted that tomorrow we're going to hear witness K4, and as I see, he is a protected witness, according to the proposal. I see no reason for an Albanian living in Kosovo to be a protected witness in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We will -- before the witness gives evidence, we will consider that position. You will have the opportunity to make your observations then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My understanding is that K4 will no longer require protective measures. I'll confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My further observation is that unless the Rule's been changed, it's a 14-day period that is required by the accused, and that has passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your knowledge, the evidence of the witness is from the villages that you will find on page 10 and 11 of the Kosovo atlas. He will mention several small villages that are on both pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you state your name, your full name, to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I'm called Asman Thaci from Demjan, born 28th of March, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you married, Mr. Thaci?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What's your profession?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I'm a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Demjan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And where is Demjan located?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Demjan is in the Has region which borders on Dedaj, Romaje, and Kushin. It's in the south of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Is it in the Prizren municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: It's in the municipality of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor during the period of 10 to 13 of November, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: On 9th of March of this year, you attended a meeting where you appeared before a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, you -- you had the opportunity to review your statement. You were given a copy of your statement in the Albanian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And after reviewing, you are able to state that the contents of your statement, they are true?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: True, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would submit the statement under Rule 92 bis, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, could you assist me in finding where is the village of Demjan on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was born in that village, but he will give evidence from the village that he passed through while he was deported, and that's what I will mention in the summary right now. But I can also help you find where he was born. If you can give me some minutes to look at the map. I will read the summary first and then I will locate it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit number 140.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness is the following: On 30 March 1999, the witness sent his family to Albania as he feared for their safety. The following day, he went to the village of Kojus - and that, Your Honour, you will see on page 11 - to attempt to persuade his father-in-law to also leave. However, while they were speaking, the village was surrounded by VJ soldiers and paramilitaries. They entered the house and told everyone to leave. The witness saw the paramilitaries grab his father-in-law, take him to a barn and set him alight with a flame-thrower before shooting him. The witness and another relative were ordered to dig a grave and bury the body. The paramilitaries took the villagers' ID documents and valuables. The witness also saw a man giving the paramilitaries money so they would not kill him. The witness joined a convoy but decided to leave it and walk to the village of Lubizhde. And, Your Honours, this village is on page 11 of the Kosovo atlas. There, he met up with a large group of displaced persons hiding in the woods. The witness remained there until 17 April 1999, when VJ soldiers surrounded them, fired their weapons. The VJ soldiers executed 17 males. They separated 50 to 100 women and girls from the group, took them 30 metres away and raped them in front of the displaced persons. The ordeal lasted for approximately two hours, during which the women and girls were slapped and verbally abused. The witness also saw a 14-year-old girl being raped in front of her family. The VJ soldiers then took the group to the village of Dedaj, where the men and the women were separated. The men were held in stables for two days before being taken to the Albanian border at Morina by buses arranged by the army. At the border, they were ordered to hand over their ID documents. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you or the villagers have any contact at all with the members of the Yugoslav army in the period between the 24th of March to the 30th of March?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: No. In our village, there was neither a headquarters nor were there members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask you about members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: There were -- about 700 metres away, there were 73 tanks. There were soldiers in the neighbourhood of Pnesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They came at the end of May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of May 1998, you say.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: True, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that they were already near your village for ten months, ten months before the events you're describing.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: And more, because on the 20th of September, 1998, they burnt Demjan, Lecine, and another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And so that means that you're claiming that from May 1998, there was the military unit with 73 tanks and all the rest of it that you enumerated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They were all the time there. They prepared for conflict, and there were no conflicts, and it was never -- there was never any kind of conflict in the two villages that are in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that during that time -- all right. During that time, you weren't an eyewitness to any conflicts or clashes between the army, the police, or anybody else. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: This area consists ethnically solely of Albanians. There were no soldiers. Nobody was killed nor were soldiers and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In that period of time, that is to say from the 24th up until the 30th of March, 1999, your village and the environments, were they bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: There was no bombing from NATO as long as we were there. There was no bombing by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see anything close by or further away, or did you hear any of the bombing that took place on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: When we left on the 17th of April, we heard when we were near the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was it that you heard then?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: There was bombing by NATO on the positions that I mentioned earlier, your positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So until -- from what I can see here, until the 17th of April, you did not hear any bombing at all; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Are you talking about my village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about you. You say that you heard the bombing for the first time on the 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: When I was in Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about the time up until the 17th of April. All I wanted to do was to see whether I had understood you correctly. Is it correct that you said that you did not hear of any NATO bombing until the 17th of April? Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I said clearly -- I said very clearly, in my village, there was no bombing during the time that I was there. And even after I left, from the 17th of April onwards, all the people had been chased away by your policemen, and we were in Albania and there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to your statement. You said that you sent two of your younger sons and wife and other two sons to Albania on the 30th of March already and that they stayed with your relatives in Albania, in Kruma. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: From the time when your Chetniks came on 29th of March, they joined your forces and they burnt houses in Grexhine, and they shelled the neighbourhood of Muhaderi, when a three-month-old child was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, I must interrupt you. We'll get on more quickly if you just concentrate on the question. The question was: Is it right that you sent two of your younger sons and your wife to Albania on the 30th of March to stay with relatives? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent them to the uncle of my father in Golaj in Albania. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did your family move from Albania to Kosovo? When did it come to settle there?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: After the liberation. They came after Kosova was liberated. I don't know when we came back, but it was after NATO ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was a different one. You have relatives, you say - your father's uncle, in fact, and other relatives - living in Kruma in Albania. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: In Golaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm asking you now is your father's uncle lives in Kruma in Albania with your other relatives then. I'm asking you: When did your family come to settle in Kosovo from Albania earlier on? I don't mean in this war, but when did they originally come to settle in Kosovo from Albania?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that? What does it matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ascertain the identity of the witness with greater precision in view of the fact that his father's uncle lives in Albania and that he has a family and relatives there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have that. But what does it matter when his family came to Albania -- came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want to do this in order to hear some -- in order to go on with my questions and to ascertain some other points. If I could get an answer to my question, please. If not, well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 1949, when the border was closed, we had no contact with our relatives in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when did you establish contact again?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: The first contact was on that day when we were expelled from our house and we went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from 1949 until 1999, you had no contact with your family in Albania?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Absolutely no contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And why didn't you send the rest of your family to Albania when you decided to send part of the family?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: You have it written very explicitly. My sons were in Montenegro. They were working in a bakery there. His wife wanted -- came, but she was blocked there, and my son didn't feel secure to come because he was afraid he would be massacred, given the fact that usually that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any member of your family a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I said even earlier, in those 52 villages, there was not a single KLA there, member or bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You lived in the municipality of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in those 52 villages of the municipality of Djakovica, there were no KLA members. That is your claim; right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Has is divided into half is in Gjakove municipality, half in Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Kojus from your village?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: My wife is from Kojus village, my spouse. The village is about 25 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did you reach Kojus from Demjan?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: In Demjan, I sheltered my family in Golaj and then I returned. I went to a friend of mine when this tragedy occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I asked you about your journey from Demjan to Kojus. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: When they expelled us, three villages, on orders from a lieutenant colonel, on the 30th of March, I took my family to Albania and then returned illegally in Kojusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the road from Demjan to Kojus, did you have any problems?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: From Albania to Kojusha, I travelled illegally, I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Kojus, were there any members of the KLA in the village?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: No. There were none of those 52 villages of Has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, how many inhabitants were in Kojus at the moment when the forces of the Yugoslav army walked in?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Kojusha is a small village. It may have about 100 inhabitants, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, was somebody else killed, apart from your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: My father-in-law was 80 years old. Met Kuka, 103-year-old, and another old man who didn't want to leave -- an old woman whose name I don't know, who didn't want to leave, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see the killing of this old man and old woman, the ones that you just referred to now?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I was there. I saw it with my own eyes. I saw the bullets flying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the answer is yes. And during these events that you describe, did you talk to any of the members of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I heard what they were saying among themselves, because we were too afraid to dare speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some Russians.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because I know some Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you speak Russian.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes, I know Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in the briefest possible terms, about the conversation that you had in the Russian language with the Russian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: This seems very ridiculous. When someone knows Serbian, it's very easy for one to understand Russian too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In your statement, you say, Mr. Thaci, the Russians were giving orders to the Yugoslav army soldiers and to the paramilitaries. Can you help us as to what those orders were?
