utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were combined. They were in a small number who communicated among themselves in Russian. And I heard with my own ears. There were -- those three men who didn't want to leave their house, I saw them when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the Russians, because you claim that there were Russians there. This is a new thing. This is the first time I hear of it. So I'm asking you about the Russians. What did you hear? Since you claim that you know the Russian language, what is this that you heard them saying?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They said, the Russians -- uh-huh. The Russians said, "We will kill others," and the army didn't allow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Did you say that these were officers who were issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I didn't see their ranks; I only saw their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that they were issuing orders in Russian. Is that right or is that not right? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: You have been wrongly informed. They didn't give orders in Russian but in Serbo-Croatian. And the conversation that several people were holding had words of Russian in it, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And how many persons were there who spoke Russian?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: About four. About four to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that some of these soldiers had the intention Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of killing Murat Athami; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: That's true. When we went on the 30th of April, 1999 to the village alongside the Drin, we were stopped by some policemen and they took this young man, Murat Athami, from a tractor, and the others, the rest of us, were maltreated and put at a distance, at a turn in the road, and we heard and saw how people produced money and saved the young man's life. And this was Murat Athami.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give money to anyone for any reason?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people were in the convoy that left the village of Kojus?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I said Kojusha has about a hundred inhabitants, but there are other villages roundabout. And we set off for Albania that day. And when we got to the customs point at Morina, they took all our documents from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us as to how many people there were in the convoy? That is what you were asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convoy, including other villagers, was a very long one, a convoy of several kilometres. I can't really say how many people there were from other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that neither the soldiers nor the members of the paramilitary forces, as you call them, followed the convoy, escorted the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why do you claim that you were fleeing from the convoy when it is true that nobody followed the convoy? Why flee then?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I fled after my son because other relatives had remained hidden in the mountains; Zenel Thaci, Bashkim Thaci, and my son Rrustem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, these relatives who were in the hills, were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: How could they be members of the KLA? They were about 3.000 people; women, old men, children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just say no.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I meant the men, the ones you mentioned staying behind in the hills. I wasn't talking about women and children. In your statement, you say that you returned to your village and that you saw there that your house had burned down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: That's right. The house was burned. Not only my house but all the other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then you go to the woods and then you return from there again to your house, you say, on the following day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why do you return yet again to your house on the very next day when it had burned down?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: To see where the young people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you met your son in the mountains on the 13th of April and that he was with your two nephews; right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: There was a large number of people. I saw by accident my son there and met him, together with Zenel and my nephew, other nephew, Bashkim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you went into the mountains because you saw smoke rising; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that these were not members of the army of Yugoslavia or the police or the paramilitary forces? This is the border area.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: The army used to patrol with armoured cars and tanks, but it was so difficult for anyone to penetrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There in the mountains on the 17th of April, you say that you encountered 2.000 refugees moving in a convoy towards Albania; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since they were moving towards Albania, why did they ask you where the road to Albania was?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Because they had come from many regions of Kosova and didn't know their way about, didn't know where to go. They didn't know the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is the Albanian border from that particular place?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Very far, because Pashtrik hill is quite a large area. It's about 2.700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who surrounded you then? Was it the army or the paramilitary forces that you mention here?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: The army and the paramilitaries surrounded us. And 17 people got killed. Five from my village, from Krasniq. The others I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the army have any losses?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: When your forces came, your lieutenant colonel came, he killed two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you describe the following situation: Two soldiers executed 17 Albanians from the convoy, and that then a lieutenant colonel of the army of Yugoslavia came and shot these two soldiers with a pistol and then they got 50 girls and women out of the convoy and raped them right there in front of you. Is that the situation that you are describing and all of these things happened one after the other?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes. They made us eat grass for about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this officer who later killed these two soldiers, where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: This lieutenant colonel, he was about one kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that he reached you from that distance; right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Where he came and where he went, I can tell you even now if I see that person. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers with him?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you've been explaining now, did all of this happen one thing after the other; that is to say, these two soldiers, as you say, execute 17 civilians, the lieutenant colonel comes, kills the two of them, and then right after, that they get 50 women out of the convoy and then they rape them collectively on the spot, they're a few metres away from you, they make you eat grass; and you describe all of that together as a single event that occurred right there on that very spot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: This happened before, the killing, the raping, and then the eating of the grass. It was very hot. There were -- there was a large crowd of people. And when this lieutenant colonel came, he killed those two notorious people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Haven't you overdone this a bit? Have you exaggerated a bit in describing everything that happened? Would you like to think about it once again?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I didn't exaggerate it at all. Everything happened as I said and the killing of those two soldiers came after what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After what?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They took us from there and took us to a barn. And after a time, they put us on buses. From the 17th of April, when we left to Albania, I know nothing about the fate of my son or the 62 persons who were left in the hands of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that you saw the killings and you saw the officer who killed the soldiers and this mass rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this. The witness has given his evidence about it, you've put it to him, you've suggested he was exaggerating, he denies it. I don't think that we can take this any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself and Haxhi Qerimi who you mentioned, did anybody else see this mass killing and rape?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: There were 3.000 people who experienced it. Haxhi Qerimi lost his son and was wounded himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the name of this 14-year-old girl was, the one that was raped by Sali Tafa?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: No. I know that she was mentally ill after this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Sali Tafa?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: He is from Kabash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: He is an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was an Albanian who raped this little 14-year-old girl.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes. He was employed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As for the rape of Albanian women and girls that you describe, did other Albanian civilians take part in this? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is -- these are your cunning fabrications. And I am not covering up either bad things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer the question, if you would. It's suggested, or rather, you're asked whether there were other Albanians involved or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was only Sali Tafa.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You know the name of Sali Tafa. Do you have any more specific information about a single Serb soldier who took part in the rape?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I saw this with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you saying that you crossed the Serbian-Albanian border in a bus at the Morina border-crossing point?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I said before: On the 17th of April, they took us away with these people from the place where this event took place to the pass of Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How; by bus?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: By bus. By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is the Morina crossing point from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: It must be about 50 or 60 kilometres. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean as the crow flies, not taking the road. As the crow flies. In a straight line.

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I'm in no position to know how far that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you stayed in Kosovo until the end of the war, or did you return to Albania?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I told you: With these people from Lubizhde in Prizren municipality, we came out on the 17th of April, and we were expelled, and we stayed in Golaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't return to Kosovo before the war ended. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I didn't go back until NATO ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you crossed the border at Morina, did anybody ask you for any ID papers?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: From everybody, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they take your ID papers away or did they keep them?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They took them away from everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you return to Kosovo ultimately?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I've told you three times. I told you three times: After NATO entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a couple of questions. Can I proceed right now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: First to clarify, Your Honour, question about the location, all the villages mentioned, they are on page 10, on the bottom of page 10. You found them?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, awhile ago you said that some of the soldiers were speaking in the Russian language. Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: They had the same uniform as the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people? Did you know any of the people speaking in the Russian language?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: I saw them there for the first time, and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaci, Sali Tafa, the Albanian person who raped the 14-year-old girl, he was an Albanian and he was a civilian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: He was with the Serbian forces although he was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Was he helping or working with the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In which capacity? What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: He was an employee of the Serbian Secret Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, you also said that you went to the Albanian border by bus. Who provided the bus?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: The Serbian army brought it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And after they brought the buses, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ASMAN THACI
utterances.text: We hadn't any problems as we went straight to the border crossing with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Romano, we've had a request from the Trial Chamber that comes in the afternoon that we finish on time in future. Of course, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we take note of it. We ought to try and get this witness through, if we can, before quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. For this witness, the Kosovo atlas page 6, and her testimony includes the municipality of Vucitrn and Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Xhevahire Rrahmani.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How old are you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I was born in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In Dubofc.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And in which municipality is Dubofc located?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And during 1999, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In Bukosh.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And that's also in the Vucitrn municipality?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Vushtrri municipality; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor during the period between the 14th to the 20th of October, 2000. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement to the members of the office?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And on 8th of March this year, you attended a meeting and appeared before an appointed officer, appointed presiding officer of this Tribunal, and you had the opportunity to review your statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you were provided with a copy of the statement in the Albanian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits the statement into evidence. The witness will testify about the following: She's a Kosovo Albanian who lived in the village of Bukos in the Vucitrn municipality. On 26 March 1999, the witness and her family went to the village of Kozica in the Srbica municipality. Serb soldiers shelled the village and started to burn the houses. The men fled to the mountains and the women were herded into a room in the house where they were robbed. The witness then went to Glogovac for ten days before returning to Kozica where she stayed until the village was again shelled by Serb forces. The VJ entered the village and rounded up the women and children who were there. They were kept in a house for two days before a group of approximately 27 women were escorted to Cirez by some of the Serb soldiers. On arrival at Cirez, the women were handed over to other soldiers who took the women to a barn. The soldiers robbed the women and then took them out, one by one, to be searched. The witness spoke to the first woman who had been searched and she told the witness that she had been stripped naked by the soldiers. One of the soldiers removed the witness from the barn. He touched her breasts and asked the witness to select a house where they could go and have sexual intercourse. The soldier harassed the witness with improper questions, showing his male organ. The witness was allowed to return to the barn without anything happening to her. The witness believes that many of the women and girls were raped. Five young women and three older women, one of whom was her mother, did not return. The eight women who did not return with them were subsequently found dead in the wells in -- in some wells in Cirez. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit number 141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since when have you been living in the village of Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Since I was married. That's 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many houses did your village have?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like with respect to security and safety during 1998 and the first three months of 1999 in your village and in the nearby villages?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: We were never left in peace, but we fled in order to avert worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about 1998 and the first three months of 1999. Were there any KLA members before the NATO aggression in your village, and did they attack the inhabitants of your village?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA in Bukosh village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember an incident that took place on the 22nd of February, 1999, in your village, the village of Bukos, when members of the KLA killed two young men, Serbs, the Milosevic brothers, at their doorstep before the eyes of their parents? Do you remember that taking place?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I heard it on the television, but I was not there and I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened in your village. And what about this other thing the next day? Do you remember that, when the OSCE observers of the Kosovo Verification Mission and numerous journalists visited that place with a police escort? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't remember. These things did happen, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It happened on the 22nd of February, the killing of those two young men. And the villagers, on the next day, that is to say, the Kosovo Verification Mission was there the next day, and the KLA shot at members of the mission too. Do you remember that? Did you hear the shooting in your village at all, both on the 22nd and on the 23rd of February?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: On 22nd of February in the evening, we left the house because there was fighting in the village, and there were forces there, but we didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 22nd, the KLA killed these two young men in your village. So you don't know anything about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to repeat that. She says she heard it on the television and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about a Serb lady by the name of Velika Vucetic from the neighbouring village of Taradza, who was kidnapped, raped by the KLA, and died as a result of burning, together with her daughter Milica? Do you know about that event taking place?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of another occurrence where members of the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of this? This witness gives very serious evidence indeed about events which occurred to her, serious crimes are alleged to have been committed against her, and you're cross-examining about totally different matters. What's the point of this if it's not simply to try and score off the witness in some way in a tit for tat? What you should be concentrating on is what the witness gave in evidence and the serious allegations which are involved there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Her statement includes the allegation that for the last 13 years prior to the NATO aggression, she lived in the village of Bukos. And as in the village of Bukos some very serious crimes took place, as she lived there for 13 years, as it is a village and not a large town, it is logical for me to ask her about the circumstances in which these -- the events which she says happened to her took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds to me as though you're simply trying to put matters to her, allegations of other crimes instead of concentrating on those that there were. It's alleged that there were crimes in the village before the events you've described in your statement. Do you know anything about these other crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was looking after my children. I didn't take an interest in these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is your answer. In due course, if you wish, you can put evidence about it, if it's relevant, about these other matters, but you should concentrate on cross-examining this witness about the things which she knows about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that she herself had said that she had lived in the village of Bukos for 13 years. So that is sufficient grounds for me to ask her about the goings-on in the village of Bukos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Xhamil Pllana, an Albanian from your village, from the village of Bukos? An Albanian. Xhamil Pllana is his name.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know of such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you perhaps heard that the man was killed by the KLA on the 4th of April, precisely in your village, the village of Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is the village Mijalic from the village of Bukos?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are concerned about this line of cross-examination. Are you trying to say that the actions about which the witness has given evidence and has made a statement, against the women in series, are you trying to say that those actions were in some way in self-defence? Otherwise, what possible relevance can it have to her evidence? Or is this a possibility: That these actions against the women in Celine were in revenge from what you say happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. Of course not. Because the alleged actions could not have been an act of self-defence, of course. But I'm speaking about the events which took place in the village in which this witness lived. And I'd like to remind you and the witness of part of her statement relating, for example -- for example -- to quote an example, to the existence of members of the Black Hand. She says, "I heard somebody mention the Black Hand when the killing took place in Likoshane, Glogovac municipality in February 1998," and so on and so forth. So she speaks about events in the neighbouring municipality, and a moment ago she just said that she knows nothing about what went on in her village because she was looking after her family. Now, if she knows nothing about what took place in her village because she was looking after her family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask her again about the Black Hand? You can ask about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that the witness, on one page, says she knows nothing except things about her family, whereas at the same time, she states that she knew what went on in the neighbouring villages. So it is logical for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask her about the Black Hand and just move on from putting these allegations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. May, whether you don't like me doing the cross-examination here, whether it bothers you, or whether you're going to tell me what I should ask the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You will cross-examine properly, and you will be limited to that. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, and that's on page 1, you say that two days after NATO began the bombing on the 26th of March, 1999, "I left my house together with my husband and children, as well as my brother-in-law by the name of Bajram and his wife Mihrije and their five children. We all went to the village of Kozica, which is where we stayed for three nights." My question is as follows: Because of what NATO operations did, did you decide to leave your village and seek refuge in the village of Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. That day, we were in Vushtrri, it was bombed. Some people were killed. We left the place. We went home. We were afraid to stay on because of the Serb police and militia who were stationed nearby our house, and we went to Kozhnice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see the bombing of Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was shelling, in fact, of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also say, in mentioning the shellings of Serb soldiers, that seven people were killed. They tried to administer first aid to the wounded, and a doctor was with them. Now, who attempted to give -- administer first aid to the wounded, and what doctor, whose doctor, which doctor?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I don't know. I know they were Serb soldiers. I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was a woman who left behind a small child, from Kozhnice village. I don't know her name. There were also some others; an old woman, a young man. There were about ten, seven, eight, or ten altogether. I didn't want my children to see what was happening and went a little further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These Serb soldiers who tried -- these Serb soldiers who tried to help the wounded, did they help the wounded Serbs or the wounded Albanians?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: First they shelled us, and they tried to provide the first aid to who remained alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said: "Three days later, the Serb forces shelled the village, and then all the men took to the mountains, Mount Cicavica, in fact." Can you explain why all the men went to Cicavica mountain and left the women and children in the village of Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because they were afraid that if they were found there, they would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Over the next ten days, from Mount Cicavica, could you hear explosions or shooting?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. They shelled, but I don't know from Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After staying in Glogovac, and you say you stayed there for ten days, you stated, "After that, we went back to Kozica because we had no food. When I went back to Kozica I found my husband there." Then you go on to say: "All the men came down from the mountain and met us there." My question is the following: Did your husband Xhavid tell you what he was doing during those ten days with all the men on Mount Cicavica? Did you ask him that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They stayed there because they felt safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What made them come back, then, if they were safer there? Why would they want to return to the village of Kozica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: To get food supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, you talk about the uniforms of the Yugoslav army. You say dark-green/light-green uniforms, and then you say, "They were probably regular soldiers belonging to the Yugoslav army." That is a quotation from your statement. Do you maintain that today? Do you still say that that was a description of the uniform worn by the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you say that the soldiers' conduct towards you was proper when you were in Durmishi's house, that they brought you food, they brought you clothing, and that they gave you some medicines for your sick daughter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms that those 25 soldiers were wearing? You said there were approximately that number. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: The soldiers were dressed in green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage, patterned uniforms, or just green?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. You mean in Cirez or in Kozhnice village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking about those soldiers, the soldiers that helped you, who brought you the food, the water, and the medicines for your daughter. What kind of uniforms were they wearing? You said they wore green uniforms. Now I'm asking you whether a plain green or did they have some patterns on them?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the soldier who told you to go to Cirez, when he advised you to do that, was he speaking in Serbian or in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: There was a young girl who knew the language. Her name was Miridite. She talked with him, and then she told us that they were going to send us to Cirez. We were sitting in two rooms on the first floor. From there, they took us to Cirez. The second room -- those who were in the second room left after three, four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This young girl, did she tell you what the man had suggested, that is, to go to Cirez? Did she say that it sounded like a threat or like a well-intentioned piece of advice? Can you make the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. She merely told us that, "You will be the first to leave, and then we will follow soon after, two or three days." Because the Serb soldier had told her that a war will take place in Cicavica and, "You will be safer there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during those two days, apart from the soldier, did you notice any officers?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In the yard of the house where we were staying, there were some. They had some ranks. I don't know what kind of ranks those were, but, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you -- you're not able to say what rank these officers held; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, I can't. But the fact is that they had those epaulettes with stars. I don't know. They had some bands on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what the soldier said, that your group should move to Cirez and the fact that Miridite didn't give the reasons for this, did you ask any of the soldiers or officer who were in command of those soldiers the reasons for that, why you had to go? When I say "you," I don't mean just you personally but anybody from your group, including you.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No. We didn't know how to talk with them, those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, you say that three soldiers escorted you to the village of Cirez and that there, there were ten soldiers, you say, in brown/black camouflage uniforms and that one of them had five stars on his shoulder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure these were brown/black camouflage uniforms and that this man had five stars on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody ever say to you that there were no such ranks in the army with five stars and these brown/black camouflage uniforms? Even after that, if you talked to somebody about it, did anybody ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6 of your statement, you say that you were taken out one by one, all of you who were in the barn, except for Ajete Ademi and Bukurije Ademi, and you say that one of the soldiers -- well, you give a kind of a description of a solder. You say he was tall, about two metres, shaved head but that he was blond, he wore the same kind of uniform like everybody else. "I did not notice any insignia or rank." This blonde soldier, is that the same soldier that you describe on page 7 as the blonde man who kept talking Albanian to you? You stated, as far as he's concerned, "He pretended not to be him but we recognised his voice and his blonde hair." Is it one and the same man?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what your answer is. Yes what? Yes, it is the same soldier?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, the same soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, he wasn't an Albanian, but he spoke Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me now, on the basis of what did you conclude that Lumnije, Zahide, Bukurije, Mirishahe, et cetera - the five girls you mentioned - that they were raped when they were taken out of the barn, although you say here, I'm quoting your words: "I did not hear a single one of them when they took them out. I could not see what was happening to them." How did you conclude that when none of them had said that to you, according to your very own statement?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Because of what they said to us and how they looked. I realised that they hadn't been -- that they had been maltreated in this way. And some of them were killed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... say that to you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me, but the young girl, Zahide Xhema, whom I talked to after the soldiers who had brought us to the barn came back, said to us, "Oh, dear. Oh, God. What has happened to us? In whose hands have we fallen?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the soldiers in the village of Kozica, where you went to later, didn't they ask you anything about these strange allegedly soldiers from Cirez? Didn't they ask you who these soldiers were, what kind of uniforms they had, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They asked us, but they knew into whose hands they had put us. The soldiers who had escorted us to Cirez were still there when we returned from Kozhnice. They were in front of a house but not Aberdin's [phoen], lower down. And they said to the women that the soldiers who had escorted us didn't want to meet them. I just wanted to tell him what happened to us, but he went inside. He didn't want to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, you said that you could not talk to them because you didn't speak the language. In which language did you wish to speak to them?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: I wanted to say to him in sign language, in any possible way, that I wanted to tell him, "You sent us there, and you know what happened to those girls and to my mother as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I understood your statement - this is on page 8 - to mean that they asked you who these soldiers were and what kind of uniforms they had. Do you know why they asked you that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. They asked us. In the afternoon, they took us, those -- the other soldiers, not the first ones, and took us again to Cirez. When we arrived there, I beckoned to one of the soldiers, telling him, "This is where they took those girls away." But he said to me, "Move on. Move on. I know."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Please, let us do this carefully. Isn't that an answer, that the soldiers of the regular army of Yugoslavia that you were in contact with - you were describing it just now - that they had their doubts as to what kind of a formation this was, these people in Cirez who were introducing themselves as belonging to some kind of an army. And then, together with you, they went back to Cirez to see what had happened to the women and girls. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. They returned, but they didn't want us to tell them exactly what happened or where those girls were taken to. They took us to another house belonging to someone called Sherif - I don't know the surname - in Cirez village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during the three weeks in Cirez, as you say, didn't these soldiers bring you food, flour for you to bake bread, diapers for the children? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They brought us bread, brought us diapers for the children. There Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was a storehouse with humanitarian aid nearby, and they did bring the supplies to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now after three weeks spent in Cirez, the soldiers told you to go to Glogovac because Cirez would be attacked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they say to you? Who would attack Cirez? Who was expected to attack?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: They said to us that it -- there will be shelling and we want to take you to Gllogoc and, from there, to go to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they say to you then that over there, nearby in Cicavica, that there was a major concentration of the KLA and that there would be intensive war operations there in that area of yours? Did they explain that to you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you left that particular place so that you would not be exposed to war operations that were expected to take place.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that, that supposedly we would send you to Macedonia, and that's what happened. And they went. I don't know how buses went in our group, but we didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay. Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, when asked awhile ago, you said that on the 26th of March, when you left your village, you were afraid to stay home because of the Serb forces and militia which were stationed nearby your house. Why were you afraid of them? What were they doing that made you afraid?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: In Bukosh, in the yards -- in the yard of a house, they killed someone called Islam. He was about 50, 55 years old. I don't know his surname. And also Hyseni, and also a young -- an only son. They killed him in the yard of a house, and so we were scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You were scared that that could happen to you as well?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE RRAHMANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Rrahmani, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution will call Mr. Abullah Salihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we've got quarter of an hour. We could make a start, at least, and you could call the witness and introduce him, and then we'll have cross-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. And I believe Ms. Romano has one item she'd like to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano, would you like to raise it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to confirm that the witness K4 won't require any protective measures for tomorrow. And in relation to his statements, they are in the process of being attested under Rule 92 bis right now and will be served mid or late this afternoon. The witness also, when he arrived this afternoon, he gave additional information amplifying the facts that was in the first two statements, and this new material in any form, a statement or notes, will be served as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Saxon. Perhaps you can help us with the atlas while we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise. The next witness will deal with events that are related to pages 05 and 06 of the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Abullah Salihu?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, were you born on the 17th of January, 1954?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Baks in the municipality of Skenderaj in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is the municipality -- excuse me. Is the village of Baks located about 11 kilometres to the east of the town of Skenderaj?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, did you provide a statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 24th of October in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was this statement about events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in March of this year, the 12th of March, 2002, in the village of Baks, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made in October of 2000 in the presence of members of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, did you attest that the copy of the statement provided to you was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Recently, in conversations with members of the Office of the Prosecutor, have you become aware of an error in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. I became aware there was an error. It was 200.000 instead of 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, just let me ask you some questions so we can get through this quickly and clearly, please. Let's talk about that error. I believe it's on page 2 of your statement, the first page that contains actual text. And in the fourth paragraph of that page, in the middle, there is a sentence that reads like this: "At the end of the two days' offensive, about 200.000 people were gathered in Cicavica." Should that number be 20.000 rather than 200.000?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, it should be 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So that sentence should read: "At the end of the two days' offensive, about 20.000 people were gathered in Cicavica"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that we don't have copies to provide to you at this time, so I'm not going to offer this statement as an exhibit at this time. I will do that tomorrow morning, first thing. Will you allow me, please, simply to use the time to read the summary of this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu serves as imam in the village of Baks where he has lived all of his life. He is married with four children. In his statement, Mr. Salihu describes the first two-day Serb offensive in his area in September of 1998 which covered the area of Gllogoc up to Skenderaj. During this offensive, many houses in the village of Baks were set on fire and most villagers left for the Cicavica mountains. About 20.000 people from the villages of this area gathered in Cicavica, and the witness estimated that 180 to 190 persons from this area died in that offensive. Mr. Salihu estimates that 80 per cent of the population from that area then spent the winter in accommodation provided by international organisations. After the OSCE withdrew from Kosovo in March 1999, paramilitaries and regular VJ soldiers with heavy armaments were deployed in the village of Cirez and Baks until June 1999. Mr. Salihu describes how the shelling by these Serb forces compelled people residing in the area to seek shelter in the woods. On the 29th of April, 1999, the Serbs launched a new offensive in the area. They shelled and surrounded the woods at a place called Fush e Molles where many civilians were hiding. Mr. Salihu tells how he and 11 others were captured by paramilitary soldiers, beaten and made to lie down on the ground and threatened that a tank would then drive over them. Due to NATO planes flying overhead at that time, the tank withdrew, and Mr. Salihu's group eventually joined other captured men and were marched off to the mosque in Cirez. Mr. Salihu was beaten, along with others, in the yard of the mosque. Mr. Salihu was one of 176 civilian men who were then forced inside the mosque, which had been burnt during a previous offensive. On the 30th of April, 1999, the detained men were beaten and lined up. One Serb military officer in charge said that he was looking for a certain Bosnian man named Mirsad. He accused the witness, Mr. Salihu, of being this person, beat him and threatened him with a pistol. Other detainees were also beaten at that time. Mr. Salihu was then ordered into a truck, one of three trucks, and taken to a place called Shavarina. Here Mr. Salihu saw between 27 and 30 persons taken off the first truck, lined up and machine-gunned into a pit. After these executions, a military jeep arrived and the two remaining trucks of captured men continued on to Gllogoc. On arrival at the police station in Gllogoc, Mr. Salihu was severely beaten, leaving him with broken ribs, a swollen knee, and legs. His group of captured men was then placed inside the Gllogoc cinema. Mr. Salihu describes how, on the second day in that cinema, a man from his group was executed by a paramilitary who selected whoever he wanted to to kill from that group. The next day, Mr. Salihu described how, when facing a wall, he heard shots behind him and how he was later ordered to put the body of a dead person in a burnt house. Mr. Salihu was kept at the police station for six days and beaten daily, and interrogated for information about the KLA. He and others captured with him and detained had no food for six days. On the seventh day, military trucks collected Mr. Salihu and other men where they were taken to the village of Bukos where he and others were forced to work for VJ reserve forces. He was able to return home when Serb forces withdrew from Kosovo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, we have to adjourn now for the day. We'll ask you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 to conclude your evidence. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your evidence, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of May, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
